# File: README.md

# Codefang

<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/uast.png" alt="Codefang Logo" width="250">
</p>

[![CI](https://github.com/Sumatoshi-tech/codefang/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Sumatoshi-tech/codefang/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![License: Apache 2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache_2.0-blue.svg)](LICENSE)

**The heavy lifter for your codebase — deep code analysis through structure and history.**

Codefang understands your code as structure (an abstract syntax tree) and as
history (Git), not just as text. It ships two binaries: `uast` parses source
into a Universal Abstract Syntax Tree across 60+ languages, and `codefang` runs
static and history analyzers over that structure and over Git repositories.

For deep dives — architecture, per-analyzer references, the metric models — see
the [documentation site](https://sumatoshi-tech.github.io/codefang/) (built from
`site/` with MkDocs Material).

---

## What it does

- **UAST parsing** — `uast` turns source code into one normalized tree shape,
  so a single analyzer works across Go, Python, JavaScript, Rust, Java, C++ and
  more (Tree-sitter under the hood).
- **Static analysis** — complexity, cohesion, comments, clones, composition,
  Halstead, and imports, computed from the UAST.
- **History analysis** — burndown, developers, couples, file-history, imports,
  quality, sentiment, shotness, typos, and anomaly, computed by walking Git
  history through libgit2.
- **Stable machine output** — `--format json` (and `yaml`, `ndjson`,
  `timeseries`, `bin`, `text`, `compact`, `plot`). The machine formats are a
  stable contract, pinned by CLI-level end-to-end tests (see Testing below).

## Why

The original `hercules` mined Git history at scale but understood code only as
diffs. Codefang keeps the history mining and adds a structural layer (the UAST),
so one analyzer reasons about meaning across many languages. The project is now
a Rust workspace; the original Go implementation has been removed.

---

## Install / build

Codefang is a single Rust workspace rooted at the repository root. You need a
recent stable Rust toolchain and a C toolchain (a C/C++ compiler and CMake) —
the `git2` crate builds a vendored copy of **libgit2** from
`third_party/libgit2`, so no system libgit2 is required.

The quickest path — clone, then one `make install` that builds both binaries
and puts them on your `PATH` (`~/.cargo/bin`):

```bash
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/Sumatoshi-tech/codefang.git
cd codefang
make install
```

`make install` also initializes the submodule, so if you cloned without
`--recurse-submodules` it still works. Run `make help` to see the other targets
(`build`, `test`, `clean`).

Prefer plain cargo, or just want the binaries in `target/release/` without
touching `PATH`? Use `make build` (equivalently
`cargo build --release -p codefang -p uast`) and invoke them by full path.

Check the install:

```console
codefang version
```

```console
uast version
```

---

## Usage

`uast` and `codefang` are separate tools (see [ADR-0002](docs/adr/0002-two-binary-split-uast-codefang.md)).

Parse a source file into a UAST:

```console
uast parse main.rs
```

Run a static analyzer over a checkout (UAST is built internally per file):

```console
codefang run --analyzers static/complexity --format json --head /path/to/repo
```

Run a history analyzer by walking Git history (use `--limit` to cap commits):

```console
codefang run --analyzers history/burndown --format json --limit 50 /path/to/repo
```

List every analyzer ID:

```console
codefang run --list-analyzers
```

Analyzer IDs are `static/<name>` and `history/<name>`; `-a` accepts globs
(`static/*`, `history/*`, `*`).

---

## Testing

Three gates, all runnable locally and all required to be green:

```bash
make test       # the workspace test suite (unit, integration, CLI-level e2e)
make lint       # clippy across the workspace; every warning is an error
make deadcode   # fails on any unreachable private item
```

The analyzer crates carry unit tests for their metric math; `bins/codefang/tests`
drives the real binary over hermetic fixture repositories and source trees and
pins the machine-format bytes end to end.

The CLI examples in this README and in `docs/` are themselves executed against
the built Rust binary by the `doc-examples` test crate
(`cargo test -p doc-examples`), so the commands shown here are runnable, not
illustrative.

# File: site/getting-started/quickstart.md

# Quick start

This page shows the fastest path to useful results. In five minutes you will
parse code, run static analysis, and mine Git history.

!!! tip "Prerequisites"
    Make sure both `codefang` and `uast` are installed.
    See [Installation](installation.md) if you have not set them up yet.

---

## 1. Parse source code into a UAST

Start by parsing a single file into a Universal Abstract Syntax Tree:

```bash
uast parse main.go
```

??? example "Expected output (truncated)"

    ```json
    {
      "language": "go",
      "file": "main.go",
      "root": {
        "type": "SourceFile",
        "roles": ["File"],
        "children": [
          {
            "type": "PackageClause",
            "roles": ["Package", "Declaration"],
            "props": { "name": "main" }
          },
          {
            "type": "FunctionDeclaration",
            "roles": ["Function", "Declaration"],
            "props": { "name": "main" },
            "children": [ "..." ]
          }
        ]
      }
    }
    ```

You can parse entire directories, force a language, or read from stdin:

```bash
uast parse --all                      # every source file in the codebase
uast parse -l python script.sh        # force Python language detection
cat main.go | uast parse -            # read from stdin
```

---

## 2. Static analysis

Run structural analysis on a folder. The `codefang run` command with
`static/*` analyzers walks the directory, parses every supported file, and
computes metrics:

```bash
codefang run -a static/complexity --format text .
```

??? example "Expected output"

    ```
    Codefang -- Code Analysis Report
    ===============================

    static/complexity:
      crates/cf-framework/src/runner.rs
        Function run_pipeline       -- Cyclomatic: 12  Cognitive: 8
        Function init_workers       -- Cyclomatic: 4   Cognitive: 3
      crates/cf-commands/src/run.rs
        Function run                -- Cyclomatic: 9   Cognitive: 7
    ```

!!! tip "Multiple static analyzers"
    Combine several analyzers in one pass:

    ```bash
    codefang run -a static/complexity,static/halstead,static/cohesion --format text .
    ```

---

## 3. History analysis -- burndown

Analyze how code ages and survives over your repository's lifetime:

```bash
codefang run -a history/burndown --format yaml .
```

??? example "Expected output (truncated)"

    ```yaml
    burndown:
      granularity: 30
      sampling: 30
      project:
        - [0, 1200, 1100, 980, 920, 870]
        - [0, 0, 320, 290, 270, 250]
        - [0, 0, 0, 180, 160, 140]
      ticks:
        - "2024-01-15"
        - "2024-02-14"
        - "2024-03-15"
        - "2024-04-14"
        - "2024-05-14"
        - "2024-06-13"
    ```

Each row in `project` represents lines added in a given time window; each
column shows how many of those lines survive into subsequent windows.

---

## 4. Developer analysis

See per-developer contribution statistics for the latest commit:

```bash
codefang run -a history/devs --head --format yaml .
```

??? example "Expected output (truncated)"

    ```yaml
    codefang (v2):
      version: 0
      hash: <unknown>
    history/devs:
    aggregate:
        total_commits: 1
        total_lines_added: 2
        total_lines_removed: 0
        total_developers: 1
        active_developers: 1
    developers:
        - id: 0
          name: alice
          email: alice@example.com
          commits: 1
          lines_added: 2
          lines_removed: 0
          lines_changed: 0
          net_lines: 2
          languages:
            - language: Go
              added: 2
              removed: 0
              changed: 0
    ```

!!! info "The `--head` flag"
    `--head` analyzes exactly one commit — `HEAD`, diffed against its first
    parent — and ignores `--limit` and `--since`. It is the same window
    `--limit 1` selects, so the two produce identical reports. Use it for a
    fast snapshot of the latest change; drop it to walk the full history.

---

## 5. Run everything at once

Use glob patterns to run all history analyzers (or all analyzers) in a single
invocation:

=== "All history analyzers"

    ```bash
    codefang run -a "history/*" --format json .
    ```

=== "All static analyzers"

    ```bash
    codefang run -a "static/*" --format json .
    ```

=== "Everything"

    ```bash
    codefang run -a "*" --format json .
    ```

!!! tip "JSON output for scripting"
    JSON is the default format and the most machine-friendly. Pipe it into
    `jq` for quick exploration:

    ```bash
    codefang run -a history/burndown --format json . | jq '.burndown.ticks'
    ```

---

## 6. Interactive HTML plots

Generate a self-contained HTML report with interactive charts:

```bash
codefang run -a history/burndown,history/devs --format plot -o report .
```

`-o` names the output **directory** (required with `--format plot`). It
receives `index.html`, one page per analyzer (`burndown.html`, `devs.html`)
and `report.json`. Open the index in your browser:

```bash
xdg-open report/index.html  # Linux
open report/index.html      # macOS
```

---

## 7. Pipe into AI

Any `--format json` output is machine-friendly and can be fed to an LLM or an
agent. Codefang also provides a **Model Context Protocol** server (the `cf-mcp`
crate) so agents can query analysis results programmatically; see the
[MCP Integration](../integrations/mcp.md) guide for how to wire it up.

!!! note "AI-ready output"
    Any `--format json` output can also be fed directly to an LLM for
    summarization or code review:

    ```bash
    codefang run -a static/complexity --format json . | llm "summarize the complexity hotspots"
    ```

---

| Set up CI/CD pipelines | [Docker & GitHub Actions](../integrations/docker-and-actions.md) |

# File: site/how-to/analyze-a-monorepo.md

# How to analyze a monorepo

<!-- Template: Good Docs Project how-to (CC-BY 4.0) — https://github.com/thegooddocsproject/templates -->

## Goal

Run Codefang against a single large repository that holds many languages and
services, and get a clean per-service report without drowning in vendored or
generated noise.

## Prerequisites

- `codefang` and `uast` installed. See [Installation](../getting-started/installation.md).
- A monorepo checked out locally, with full Git history (history analyzers need
  every commit, not a shallow clone).
- `jq` if you want to post-process the JSON output.

## Steps

1. Run static analysis across the whole tree first. By default Codefang already
   excludes vendored dependencies (`vendor/`, `node_modules/`, `third_party/`,
   `testdata/`) and generated files, so the report covers your own code only:

   ```bash
   codefang run -a 'static/*' --format json --silent .
   ```

2. Narrow a noisy polyglot repo to the languages you care about. The
   `--languages` filter applies to both the static and history phases and skips
   non-matching files before they are parsed:

   ```bash
   codefang run -a 'static/*' --languages go,typescript,python --format json .
   ```

3. Scope a run to a single service directory instead of the whole repo by
   passing its path (or `--path`):

   ```bash
   codefang run -a 'static/complexity,static/cohesion' --format json ./services/api
   ```

4. Add extra exclusion prefixes for tooling directories that Linguist's
   heuristics do not catch, such as a Python virtualenv or a Rust target dir:

   ```bash
   codefang run -a '*' --extra-excluded-prefixes '.venv/,target/,build/' --format json .
   ```

5. Bound the history window on a large monorepo — there is no memory or
   worker knob; a history run costs what its commit window costs. Limit the
   range with `--since` or `--limit`, skip merge side branches with
   `--first-parent`, and drop mass-change commits (vendoring dumps,
   generated-code regenerations) with `--max-changes-per-commit`:

   ```bash
   codefang run -a 'history/*' --limit 5000 --first-parent --format json --silent .
   ```

6. If you need only a period of the history, select it with `--since`:

   ```bash
   codefang run -a 'history/devs' --since 2025-01-01 --format json .
   ```

## Result

You have a JSON report scoped to your own source code (vendored and generated
files excluded) and, when you narrow by `--languages` or path, scoped to the
service you care about. Confirm the scope by inspecting the report — for
example, count the files Codefang actually analyzed:

```bash
codefang run -a 'static/complexity' --languages go --format json . | jq '.["static/complexity"] | length'
```

## See also

- [How to run Codefang in CI](run-in-ci.md)
- [Large-scale repository scanning](../operations/large-scale-scanning.md)
- [CLI reference](../guide/cli-reference.md)

# File: site/how-to/run-in-ci.md

# How to run Codefang in CI

<!-- Template: Good Docs Project how-to (CC-BY 4.0) — https://github.com/thegooddocsproject/templates -->

## Goal

Add Codefang to a continuous-integration pipeline so every push and pull request
runs code analysis automatically, and optionally fail the build when analysis
detects issues.

## Prerequisites

- A repository hosted on GitHub (this guide uses the published GitHub Action).
- Permission to add workflow files under `.github/workflows/`.
- For history analyzers, the checkout step must fetch full history
  (`fetch-depth: 0`); a shallow clone only sees the most recent commits.

## Steps

1. Create `.github/workflows/codefang.yml` and add the action with the
   analyzers you want. Static analysis works on a shallow clone:

   ```yaml
   name: Code Quality
   on: [push, pull_request]

   jobs:
     analyze:
       runs-on: ubuntu-latest
       steps:
         - uses: actions/checkout@v4

         - name: Run Codefang
           id: codefang
           uses: Sumatoshi-tech/codefang@main
           with:
             analyzers: "static/*"
             format: "json"
   ```

2. Turn the run into a quality gate by setting `fail-on-error: "true"`. The step
   fails the workflow when analysis detects issues:

   ```yaml
         - name: Run Codefang
           uses: Sumatoshi-tech/codefang@main
           with:
             analyzers: "static/complexity,static/comments"
             fail-on-error: "true"
   ```

3. For history analyzers, fetch the full Git history in the checkout step,
   otherwise the analysis only sees the shallow clone:

   ```yaml
         - uses: actions/checkout@v4
           with:
             fetch-depth: 0

         - name: Run Codefang History
           uses: Sumatoshi-tech/codefang@main
           with:
             analyzers: "history/burndown,history/devs"
             format: "json"
   ```

4. Read the action outputs in a later step. `pass` is `true` when analysis
   completed without errors, and `report` holds the full report content:

   ```yaml
         - name: Check results
           run: |
             echo "Pass: ${{ steps.codefang.outputs.pass }}"
             echo "${{ steps.codefang.outputs.report }}"
   ```

5. If a large repository runs out of memory or time in CI, bound the history
   window — `--limit`, `--since`, `--first-parent`,
   `--max-changes-per-commit` — by running the binary directly inside the
   job, or in Docker:

   ```bash
   docker run --rm -v "$(pwd):/workspace:ro" \
     codefang run -a 'history/*' --limit 2000 --format json --silent /workspace
   ```

## Result

Open the Actions tab after a push. The Codefang job runs, prints the report, and
— when `fail-on-error` is set — marks the check red if analysis detected issues.
A green check with a populated `report` output confirms the pipeline works.

## See also

- [Docker & GitHub Actions reference](../integrations/docker-and-actions.md)
- [How to analyze a monorepo](analyze-a-monorepo.md)
- [Output formats](../guide/output-formats.md)

# File: site/how-to/read-a-burndown-chart.md

# How to read a burndown chart

<!-- Template: Good Docs Project how-to (CC-BY 4.0) — https://github.com/thegooddocsproject/templates -->

## Goal

Generate a code-survival burndown for a repository and interpret the result so
you can see how much code from each era still survives at the latest sample.

## Prerequisites

- `codefang` installed and a Git repository checked out with full history.
- A web browser to view the interactive HTML chart.
- `jq` if you want to inspect the raw matrix.

## Steps

1. Run the burndown analyzer and write the YAML output so you can read the raw
   matrix:

   ```bash
   codefang run -a history/burndown --format yaml .
   ```

2. Read the `project` matrix. Each row is a sampling point in time; each value
   in a row is the number of lines, created in a given age band, that still
   survive at that sample. As you read down the rows, watch a band's values
   shrink — that is code being rewritten or deleted over time:

   ```yaml
   burndown:
     granularity: 30
     sampling: 30
     project:
       - [0, 1200, 1100, 980, 920, 870]
       - [0, 0, 320, 290, 270, 250]
     ticks:
       - "2024-01-15"
       - "2024-02-14"
   ```

3. Use `ticks` to map matrix positions back to calendar dates. The `granularity`
   key is the width of each age band (in ticks) and `sampling` is how often a
   snapshot is taken; the default tick is a 24-hour window.

4. Add a per-developer breakdown to see whose code survives, by enabling
   developer tracking:

   ```bash
   codefang run -a history/burndown --burndown-people --format yaml .
   ```

5. Generate the interactive stacked-area chart and open it in a browser. This is
   the visual form of the same matrix:

   ```bash
   codefang run -a history/burndown --format plot -o burndown .
   xdg-open burndown/index.html   # Linux
   open burndown/index.html       # macOS
   ```

6. Extract just the tick axis for scripting or a custom plot:

   ```bash
   codefang run -a history/burndown --format json . | jq '.burndown.ticks'
   ```

## Result

You can point at any value in the chart or matrix and state what it means: "this
many lines, written around this date, still survive at this later date." A
declining survival curve signals churn; a flat top band signals stable,
long-lived code.

## See also

- [Understanding code burndown](../explanation/burndown.md) — the mental model.
- [Burndown reference](../analyzers/burndown.md) — configuration keys and output schema.
- [How to run Codefang in CI](run-in-ci.md)

# File: site/how-to/analyze-a-bare-repo.md

# How to analyze a bare repository

<!-- Template: Good Docs Project how-to (CC-BY 4.0) — https://github.com/thegooddocsproject/templates -->

## Goal

Run history analysis directly against a bare Git repository — such as a GitLab
backup, a Gitolite mirror, or a `git clone --bare` mirror — without first
checking out a working tree.

## Prerequisites

- `codefang` installed.
- A bare repository on disk (a directory ending in `.git` with no working tree).
- For GitLab backups, enough disk space to extract the `repositories/` tree.

## Steps

1. Point `codefang run` directly at the bare repository path. Codefang uses
   libgit2, which opens bare and non-bare repositories transparently, so no
   clone or checkout is required:

   ```bash
   codefang run /data/backups/repositories/@hashed/ab/cd/abcdef.git \
     -a 'history/*' --format json --silent
   ```

2. To scan a GitLab backup, extract the repositories tree from the tarball:

   ```bash
   tar xf backup.tar -C /data/extract repositories/
   ```

3. Build a list of real project repos, skipping wiki and design repos:

   ```bash
   find /data/extract/repositories -name "*.git" \
     ! -name "*.wiki.git" \
     ! -name "*.design.git" \
     -type d > /tmp/repo_paths.txt
   ```

4. Run a single bare repo; bound the commit window with `--limit` on large
   histories:

   ```bash
   codefang run /data/extract/repositories/@hashed/ab/cd/abcdef.git \
     -a 'history/*' --limit 5000 --format json --silent
   ```

5. For periodic scans, analyze only new commits with `--since` rather than
   re-walking the whole history each run:

   ```bash
   codefang run /data/extract/repositories/@hashed/ab/cd/abcdef.git \
     -a 'history/*' --since 168h --format json --silent
   ```

## Result

You get the same history report you would get from a normal working clone —
burndown, developers, couples, and more — produced straight from the bare repo
with no checkout. A non-empty JSON report on stdout confirms the bare repo was
opened and analyzed.

## See also

- [Large-scale repository scanning](../operations/large-scale-scanning.md)
- [How to analyze a monorepo](analyze-a-monorepo.md)
- [CLI reference](../guide/cli-reference.md)

# File: site/how-to/attach-an-mcp-client.md

# How to attach an MCP client

<!-- Template: Good Docs Project how-to (CC-BY 4.0) — https://github.com/thegooddocsproject/templates -->

## Goal

Connect an AI agent to Codefang over the Model Context Protocol (MCP) so the
agent can run code analysis as a tool.

## Prerequisites

- `codefang` installed and on your `PATH`.
- An MCP-compatible client (for example, Claude Code or another agent that
  launches MCP servers over stdio).
- For the `codefang_history` tool, an absolute path to a local Git repository.

!!! warning "Not available in this release"
    No `codefang` subcommand launches the MCP server yet: `codefang mcp`
    fails with `unrecognized subcommand 'mcp'`. The server and its tools are
    implemented in the `cf-mcp` library crate (see [MCP server](../integrations/mcp.md));
    these steps describe the integration once a launcher ships.

## Steps

1. Confirm the MCP server starts. It communicates over stdio using JSON-RPC, the
   standard transport for local MCP tool use:

   ```bash
   codefang mcp
   ```

   Press `Ctrl-C` to stop it — the agent will launch its own copy.

2. Register Codefang as an MCP server in your client. For Claude Code, add it to
   `~/.claude/settings.json` (user scope) or `.claude/settings.json` (project
   scope):

   ```json
   {
     "mcpServers": {
       "codefang": {
         "command": "codefang",
         "args": ["mcp"],
         "env": {}
       }
     }
   }
   ```

3. Restart the client so it picks up the new server. The agent then discovers
   three tools via the standard MCP `tools/list` method: `codefang_analyze`
   (static analysis on inline code), `uast_parse` (parse source into a UAST),
   and `codefang_history` (history analysis on a local repo).

4. Ask the agent to run history analysis. The `codefang_history` tool requires
   an absolute `repo_path`; a relative path is rejected:

   ```json
   {
     "name": "codefang_history",
     "arguments": {
       "repo_path": "/home/user/projects/myapp",
       "analyzers": ["burndown", "devs"],
       "limit": 500
     }
   }
   ```

5. If a call misbehaves, enable debug logging to stderr by adding the `--debug`
   argument to the server registration:

   ```json
   {
     "mcpServers": {
       "codefang": {
         "command": "codefang",
         "args": ["mcp", "--debug"],
         "env": {}
       }
     }
   }
   ```

## Result

The agent lists the three Codefang tools and returns structured analysis when it
calls them. A successful `codefang_analyze` or `codefang_history` call that comes
back without `isError: true` confirms the client is attached.

## See also

- [MCP server reference](../integrations/mcp.md)
- [AI agents](../integrations/ai-agents.md)
- [How to read a burndown chart](read-a-burndown-chart.md)


---

# File: site/analyzers/index.md

# Analyzers

Codefang ships two families of analyzers that extract quantitative insights from your codebase.

**Static analyzers** operate on source code via UAST (Universal Abstract Syntax Tree) and evaluate structural properties of the code as it exists right now. **History analyzers** walk Git commit history and track how the codebase evolves over time.

---

## Static analyzers

Static analyzers parse source files into a UAST and compute metrics in a single pass. They require no repository history and can run on individual files or entire directory trees.

| Analyzer | ID | Description |
|---|---|---|
| [Complexity](complexity.md) | `static/complexity` | Cyclomatic complexity, cognitive complexity, nesting depth |
| [Cohesion](cohesion.md) | `static/cohesion` | LCOM over function–variable usage, function cohesion |
| [Halstead](halstead.md) | `static/halstead` | Program length, vocabulary, volume, difficulty, effort |
| [Comments](comments.md) | `static/comments` | Documentation coverage, comment placement quality |
| [Imports](imports.md) | `static/imports` | Import and dependency analysis |
| [Clones](clones.md) | `static/clones` | Cross-file duplicate function detection via MinHash + LSH |
| [Composition](composition.md) | `static/composition` | File-type breakdown: source, docs, config, vendor, generated, dotfile, image, binary, other |

### Running static analyzers

Point `codefang run` at a file or a directory tree; the UAST is built
internally per file:

```bash
# Single file, single analyzer
codefang run -a static/complexity main.go

# Entire directory tree, single analyzer
codefang run -a static/complexity ./src/

# Entire directory tree, all static analyzers
codefang run -a 'static/*' ./src/
```

Every static analyzer reads the **same** walk of the tree, so
`-a 'static/*'` reports exactly the numbers the single runs report: the
walk visits directories in lexical order (skipping `.git`, cache-tagged
directories and symlinked directories), admits the files the UAST parser
supports and `--languages` keeps, applies the vendor / generated /
`--extra-excluded-prefixes` policy to the root-relative path, reads each
file once (files over 64 MiB and unreadable files are skipped with one
stderr warning each), and applies the generated-content marker
(`DO NOT EDIT`, `Code generated`, … in the first 512 bytes) unless
`--include-generated`. `static/composition` classifies every file instead,
vendored and generated included. `--per-file` adds per-file entries to
`--format json` only. See the
[CLI reference](../guide/cli-reference.md#the-static-walk) for the full
contract.

---

## History analyzers

History analyzers iterate over Git commits (oldest to newest) and accumulate statistics about how files, developers, and code structure change over time. They require a Git repository.

| Analyzer | ID | Description |
|---|---|---|
| [Burndown](burndown.md) | `history/burndown` | Code survival over time, line ownership tracking |
| [Developers](developers.md) | `history/devs` | Developer activity, language breakdown, bus factor |
| [Couples](couples.md) | `history/couples` | File coupling, co-change patterns |
| [File History](file-history.md) | `history/file-history` | Per-file lifecycle and modification tracking |
| [Quality](quality.md) | `history/quality` | Complexity, Halstead, comment, and cohesion metrics over time |
| [Sentiment](sentiment.md) | `history/sentiment` | Comment sentiment analysis over time |
| [Shotness](shotness.md) | `history/shotness` | Structural hotspots (function-level change tracking) |
| [Typos](typos.md) | `history/typos` | Typo detection dataset builder |
| [Anomaly](anomaly.md) | `history/anomaly` | Z-score temporal anomaly detection |

### Running history analyzers

Use `codefang run` with the `-a` flag:

```bash
# Single analyzer
codefang run -a history/burndown .

# Multiple analyzers
codefang run -a history/devs -a history/couples .

# All history analyzers
codefang run -a 'history/*' .
```

---

## Glob patterns

You can select analyzers using glob patterns with the `-a` flag:

```bash
# All static analyzers
codefang run -a 'static/*' ./src/

# All history analyzers
codefang run -a 'history/*' .

# All analyzers (both static and history)
codefang run -a '*' .
```

---

## Output formats

All analyzers support multiple output formats via the `--format` flag:

=== "JSON"

    ```bash
    codefang run -a history/devs --format json .
    ```

=== "YAML"

    ```bash
    codefang run -a history/devs --format yaml .
    ```

=== "Plot"

    ```bash
    codefang run -a history/burndown --format plot .
    ```

=== "Binary"

    ```bash
    codefang run -a history/burndown --format binary .
    ```

!!! tip "Combining analyzers"
    When running multiple history analyzers together, they share the same commit walk, making combined runs significantly faster than running each analyzer separately.


---

# File: site/guide/cli-reference.md

# CLI reference

Codefang ships two binaries: **`codefang`**, the analyzer engine, and **`uast`**, the
Universal Abstract Syntax Tree parser. This page is the exhaustive reference for
every command, sub-command, and flag. Every flag listed by `codefang run --help`
is documented here and is read by the pipeline; a flag that is accepted but
has no effect is a bug.

---

## `codefang`

The main analysis binary. It runs static and history analyzers against source
code and Git repositories.

#### Global flags

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--verbose` | `-v` | `bool` | `false` | Print run details on stderr: `progress: config file: <path>` (or `none`) and `progress: analyzers: <resolved ids>` |
| `--quiet` (alias `--silent`) | `-q` | `bool` | `false` | Suppress the `progress:` lines on stderr; warnings and errors still print. `-v` and `-q` together are a usage error. |
| `--profile` | | `bool` | `false` | Memory watchdog: logs `MEM t=<s> RSS=<MiB> threads=<n>` to stderr at start and every 2 s, writes `/proc/self/maps` to `$TMPDIR/maps_baseline.txt` at start and `maps_spike_<MiB>MiB.txt` on the first RSS spike above 4096 MiB (Linux) |

Global flags are accepted before or after the subcommand
(`codefang -q run …` ≡ `codefang run -q …`).

### `codefang run`

The primary entry point. Runs selected static and/or history analyzers on a
codebase or repository.

```bash
codefang run [path] [flags]
```

If `path` is omitted the current directory (or the value of `--path`) is used.

#### Analyzer selection

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--analyzers` | `-a` | `[]string` | all | Analyzer IDs or glob patterns. Comma-separated. Omitted ⇒ every analyzer. |
| `--list-analyzers` | | `bool` | `false` | Print every analyzer ID (one per line) and exit |

Analyzer IDs follow a `<category>/<name>` convention. Globs are supported:

```bash
# Single analyzer
codefang run -a static/complexity .

# All static analyzers
codefang run -a 'static/*' .

# All history analyzers
codefang run -a 'history/*' .

# Multiple specific analyzers
codefang run -a static/complexity,history/burndown,history/devs .

# Everything
codefang run -a '*' .
```

??? info "Available Analyzer IDs"

    **Static analyzers:**
    `static/clones`, `static/cohesion`, `static/comments`, `static/complexity`,
    `static/composition`, `static/halstead`, `static/imports`

    **History analyzers:**
    `history/anomaly`, `history/burndown`, `history/couples`,
    `history/devs`, `history/file-history`, `history/imports`,
    `history/quality`, `history/sentiment`, `history/shotness`,
    `history/typos`

#### Output flags

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--format` | | `string` | `json` | Output format: `json`, `yaml`, `bin`, `text`, `compact`, `ndjson`, `timeseries`, `plot` |
| `--ndjson` | | `bool` | `false` | With `--format timeseries`: emit one JSON line per commit instead of the merged document. With any other format the run fails with `Error: invalid --ndjson: requires --format timeseries, got --format <f>`. |
| `--output` | `-o` | `string` | `""` | Write the report to this file (created or truncated) instead of stdout. With `--format plot` it is the output directory for the HTML pages, and required. |
| `--per-file` | `-F` | `bool` | `false` | Add one `files` entry per analyzed file to every static section. **`--format json` only**: with any other format the flag is ignored and the run prints `--per-file applies to --format json only; ignored for <format>` on stderr (once). |
| `--no-color` | | `bool` | `false` | Disable ANSI color in `text` / `compact` output (same as `NO_COLOR=1`) |

Which formats a selection accepts:

| Selection | Accepted formats |
|-----------|------------------|
| static only | `json`, `yaml`, `bin`, `text`, `compact`, `plot` |
| history only | `json`, `yaml`, `bin`, `text`, `compact`, `ndjson`, `timeseries` (+ `--ndjson`), `plot` |
| mixed static + history | `json`, `yaml`, `bin`, `ndjson`, `timeseries`, `plot` |

`text` is supported by the six history analyzers with a text renderer
(sentiment, shotness, burndown, couples, devs, file-history); selecting any
other history analyzer with `--format text` fails with
`serialization error for <Name>: unsupported format: text`.

```bash
# Human-readable table
codefang run -a 'static/*' --format text .

# One summary line per history analyzer
codefang run -a 'history/*' --format compact .

# Interactive HTML charts
codefang run -a 'history/*' --format plot --output ./report .

# The report in a file instead of stdout
codefang run -a static/complexity --format json -o complexity.json .

# Unified time-series JSON
codefang run -a 'history/devs,history/sentiment' --format timeseries .
```

!!! note "Several analyzers, one document"
    A `json` or `yaml` run that selects more than one analyzer — a mixed
    static+history selection, or several history analyzers — always emits
    **one** document:

    ```json
    {
      "version": "codefang.run.v1",
      "metadata": { "...": "run provenance" },
      "analyzers": [
        { "id": "history/devs", "mode": "history", "report": { "...": "the devs report" } },
        { "id": "history/burndown", "mode": "history", "report": { "...": "the burndown report" } }
      ]
    }
    ```

    A single analyzer emits its own report as the document root. Several
    **static** analyzers in `json`/`text` merge their sections into one report
    with an `overall_score`.

#### Path flags

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--path` | `-p` | `string` | `.` | Folder or repository path to analyze (the positional `path` wins when both are given) |

#### Git history flags

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--limit` | `int` | `0` | Analyze at most N commits — the N **newest** (`0` = no limit). Negative values are rejected. |
| `--since` | `string` | `""` | Only analyze commits **authored** at/after this time or revision |
| `--first-parent` | `bool` | `false` | Follow only the first parent of merge commits |
| `--head` | `bool` | `false` | Analyze only the HEAD commit (ignores `--limit` and `--since`) |
| `--tick-size` | `int` | `24` | Width of one tick in hours (must be `> 0`). Burndown bands, devs activity, anomaly windows and `commits_by_tick` are bucketed by tick. |
| `--max-changes-per-commit` | `int` | `0` | Drop commits whose raw tree diff exceeds this many changes (`0` = default 10000; negative values are rejected). Dropped commits are invisible to every analyzer; burndown re-inserts an affected file whole the next time it is touched. Raise this on monorepos with legitimate large commits. |

These flags bound the **history** phase only — static analyzers read the
working tree, so none of them affects a static run.

The window is selected **newest-first** (`--limit 10` = the ten most recent
commits, like `git log -n 10`) and then handed to the analyzers in
chronological oldest-first order, because ticks, burndown line survival and
author identity all depend on that order. `--limit` and `--since` compose:
`--since` picks the window, `--limit` caps its newest end. `--head` is the
single-commit window `[HEAD]` — the same window `--limit 1` selects, so the two
produce byte-identical reports for every analyzer and format.

The `--since` flag accepts these forms, in precedence order:

- **Duration**: `24h`, `168h` (one week), `1h30m` — units are `h`/`m`/`s`
  only. There is **no** `d` or `w` unit and `m` means **minutes**, so a week
  is `168h`, not `7d`
- **Date**: `2025-01-01` (midnight UTC)
- **RFC 3339**: `2025-01-01T00:00:00Z`
- **Git revision**: `v1.2.0`, `HEAD~100`, or a bare SHA — that commit's author
  time becomes the cutoff

The cutoff compares the commit's **author** time, and every commit authored
at/after it is kept regardless of its position in the committer-time walk
(a commit authored after the cutoff but committed before it is still
included; one authored before the cutoff but committed after it is not).

```bash
# Everything authored in the last 168h (one week)
codefang run -a history/devs --since 168h .

# Since a specific date
codefang run -a history/burndown --since 2025-01-01 .

# Since a release tag
codefang run -a history/couples --since v1.2.0 .

# Only the latest 500 commits
codefang run -a history/couples --limit 500 .

# Hourly ticks
codefang run -a history/devs --tick-size 1 --format timeseries .
```

!!! note "Empty windows and bad values"
    A `--since` cutoff newer than every commit analyzes nothing: the run
    succeeds (exit 0) and every history analyzer emits its empty report. A
    cutoff at or before the root commit filters nothing. A value that is
    neither a time form nor a resolvable revision fails immediately with
    `Error: cannot resolve --since "<value>"`, empty stdout, exit 1.

!!! note "Burndown always walks first-parent"
    The burndown analyzer tracks line survival along the main line of
    development, so **its own** walk always follows the first parent of merge
    commits, whatever `--first-parent` says. This never leaks into the other
    analyzers: selecting burndown next to devs, couples or file-history leaves
    their walks exactly as the user's `--first-parent` flag configures them.

!!! note "Renames"
    The tree diff detects renames (libgit2 `find_similar`, the `git diff -M`
    default of 50 % similarity). A pure `git mv` is one change whose old and
    new paths differ and whose blob is unchanged, so devs reports 0 added /
    0 removed lines for it and burndown, couples, file-history and shotness
    keep the file's identity across the move.

!!! note "Deterministic output"
    A history report is a pure function of the repository and the flags. It
    does not depend on the host's CPU count, the wall clock, or the number of
    threads the walk happens to use.

#### Language filtering

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--languages` | `[]string` | `[all]` | Restrict analysis to the given Linguist languages; comma-separated. `all` (default), an absent flag and an explicit empty value (`--languages ""`) all disable the filter. Applies to **both** history and static phases with one meaning. In the static phase each language resolves to its Linguist filename globs, matched against the file's **basename** (`*.go`, `*.py`, `Dockerfile`, …). |

**History phase** — each changed file is classified with the full enry
cascade over its basename **and** its blob content, so ambiguous extensions
(`.h`, `.m`, `.pl`, `.r`) and extensionless scripts (shebang) resolve
correctly; changes whose language is not in the set are dropped before any
analyzer sees them.

**Static phase** — the filter is applied by the ONE directory walk every
static analyzer shares, before the UAST parser or raw-file analyzers see the
file: the language globs are matched against the basename, so the parser's
own language router remains the final authority for how a matched file is
parsed. Both phases read the same `langpath` tables, so the flag value has
one meaning across `-a 'static/*'`, `-a 'history/*'`, and `-a '*'` runs.

#### The static walk

Every `static/*` analyzer reads the same walk of the path you pass
(a directory or a single file):

- directories are visited in lexical order, depth-first; `.git` and any
  directory carrying a `CACHEDIR.TAG` (Cargo's `target/`) are skipped;
  symlinked directories are never followed (a symlink loop cannot recurse
  and the walk cannot leave the root); symlinks to regular files are read;
- a file is admitted when the UAST parser supports its extension, its
  basename matches `--languages`, and its **root-relative** path passes the
  vendor / generated / `--extra-excluded-prefixes` policy;
- each admitted file is read **once**; a file larger than **64 MiB** or one
  that cannot be read is skipped with one stderr line
  (`warning: skipped <path>: larger than 64 MiB` / `: unreadable`) for the
  whole run, however many analyzers are selected, and counted once in the
  end-of-run `progress: skipped N unreadable/oversized/unparseable files`
  line;
- the generated-content marker (`DO NOT EDIT`, `Code generated`,
  `@generated`, … in the first 512 bytes) is applied to the bytes just read
  unless `--include-generated`;
- a single-file path analyzes that one file and stamps its **name**
  (`a.go`, never `.`) on every per-file entry and issue location.

`static/composition` is the designed exception: it exists to report
vendored / generated / binary shares, so it classifies **every** regular
file the walk reaches (reading only the first 8 KiB of each); only
`--languages` and `--extra-excluded-prefixes` narrow it.

Language names are [Linguist keys](https://github.com/github/linguist/blob/master/lib/linguist/languages.yml)
and common aliases resolve automatically:

```bash
# Canonical names (any case, whitespace is trimmed)
codefang run -a 'history/devs' --languages go,python,typescript .

# Aliases resolve via the Linguist tables
codefang run -a 'history/devs' --languages golang,js,ts .

# Unknown language fails fast instead of silently returning an empty report:
codefang run -a 'history/devs' --languages notalang .
# → Error: history --languages: unknown language: "notalang"
codefang run -a 'static/complexity' --languages notalang .
# → Error: static --languages: unknown language: "notalang"
```

Filename-only languages (e.g. `Dockerfile`, `Makefile`) are also supported:

```bash
codefang run -a 'history/devs' --languages dockerfile .
```

#### Vendor & generated exclusion

By default, Codefang excludes **vendored dependencies** and **auto-generated
files** from analysis. This matches the convention of every major
single-language analyser (`go vet`, `eslint`, `ruff`, `rubocop`, `scalafix`,
`phpcs`, …) — vendor/generated code is noise for a code-quality report.

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--include-vendored` | `bool` | `false` | Re-include vendored dependencies (detected by the Linguist vendor patterns over the **root-relative** path) in analysis. Cross-language: covers `vendor/`, `node_modules/`, `third_party/`, `testdata/`, minified bundles, and more. `static/composition` counts vendored files regardless. |
| `--include-generated` | `bool` | `false` | Re-include auto-generated files in analysis. Covers `*.pb.go`, `zz_generated_*.go`, `*_pb2.py`, `*.min.js` (path heuristics) **and** any file whose first 512 bytes contain a generated-file marker (`DO NOT EDIT`, `Code generated`, `@generated`, …) — the static walk reads every admitted file and applies the marker to it; the history filter applies it to the blob header. `static/composition` counts generated files regardless. |
| `--extra-excluded-prefixes` | `[]string` | `[]` | Additional UNIX path prefixes to exclude on top of the built-in heuristics (e.g. `".venv/,target/,build/"`), matched against the **root-relative** path (`gen/` excludes `<root>/gen/…` whatever the root spelling). Always excludes, even with the include flags set, and narrows `static/composition` too. |

All three flags apply **identically** to both static and history phases: the
history change filter reads the blob header for the generated-file marker
exactly as the static walk reads the bytes of each admitted file.

```bash
# default: your own code only
codefang run -a '*' .

# include vendored deps (node_modules/, vendor/, …)
codefang run -a '*' --include-vendored .

# include everything
codefang run -a '*' --include-vendored --include-generated .

# skip extras the heuristics do not know about (e.g. Python venv, Rust target/)
codefang run -a '*' --extra-excluded-prefixes '.venv/,target/' .
```

!!! warning "Removed spellings"
    The hidden `--skip-blacklist` and `--blacklisted-prefixes` flags were
    accepted and ignored; they are removed and fail as unknown arguments.
    Drop `--skip-blacklist` (the default already excludes) and write
    `--blacklisted-prefixes X,Y` as `--extra-excluded-prefixes X,Y`.

#### Developer identity

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--people-dict` | `path` | `""` | File with one person per line, `|`-separated identity tokens (names and emails, matched case-insensitively). With a dictionary, an author matching no line is reported as `<unmatched>`. An unreadable file is an error. |
| `--exact-signatures` | `bool` | `false` | Match the whole `name <email>` signature instead of merging authors that share a name **or** an email. Yields considerably more identities. |
| `--anonymize` | `bool` | `false` | Replace developer names in every report with `Developer-A`, `Developer-B`, … |

By default an author is identified by **either** the lowercased email or the
lowercased name, and a hit on one token registers the other: `alice <a@x>`,
`Alice Smith <a@x>` and `Alice Smith <a@y>` are one developer. One identity
detector serves every history analyzer, so devs, burndown, couples,
file-history and anomaly agree on author ids.

```
# people.txt
Alice|alice@example.com|alice@other.org
Bob|bob@example.com
```

```bash
codefang run -a history/devs --people-dict people.txt .
codefang run -a history/devs --anonymize --format text .
```

#### Analyzer options

| Flag | Type | Default | Applies to | Description |
|------|------|---------|------------|-------------|
| `--typos-max-distance` | `int` | `4` | `history/typos` | Maximum Levenshtein distance between the two identifiers of a typo-fix pair (also bounds the whole-line prefilter); must be `> 0` |
| `--granularity` | `int` | `30` | `history/burndown` | Ticks per age band of the survival matrix (must be `> 0`; `Error: invalid --granularity: must be > 0, got <v>`) |
| `--sampling` | `int` | `30` | `history/burndown` | Ticks per sample row of the survival matrix (must be `> 0`; independent of `--granularity`) |
| `--burndown-files` | `bool` | `false` | `history/burndown` | Per-file survival (`file_survival`, `tracked_files`, ndjson `FileDeltas`); with `--burndown-people` also per-file ownership |
| `--burndown-people` | `bool` | `false` | `history/burndown` | Per-developer survival and the interaction matrix (`developer_survival`, `interactions`, `tracked_developers`, ndjson `PeopleDeltas` / `MatrixDeltas`, the text "Top Developers" section) |
| `--anomaly-window` | `int` | `20` | `history/anomaly` | Trailing window size in ticks for the rolling mean and standard deviation (must be `>= 2`; a shorter history uses every earlier tick) |
| `--anomaly-threshold` | `float` | `2.0` | `history/anomaly` | Z-score threshold, in standard deviations, above which a tick is flagged (must be `> 0`) |
| `--empty-commits` | `bool` | `false` | `history/devs` | Count commits whose filtered diff is empty (trivial merges, `--allow-empty` commits, commits touching only excluded paths) as commits with zero lines |
| `--shotness-dsl-struct` | `string` | `rfilter(.roles has "Function")` | `history/shotness` | UAST DSL query selecting the tracked declarations anywhere in each file (`filter(...)` would see the top level only); validated before the walk, an invalid expression is a flag error |
| `--shotness-dsl-name` | `string` | `.props.name` | `history/shotness` | UAST DSL query extracting a declaration's own name (applied to selected nodes and their enclosing declarations); validated before the walk |
| `--min-comment-len` | `int` | `20` | `history/sentiment` | Minimum comment length in characters to analyze; `0` disables the length filter, a negative value is rejected (`Error: invalid --min-comment-len: …`) |

#### Configuration

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--config` | `string` | `""` | Configuration file. Without it `./.codefang.yaml`, then `$HOME/.codefang.yaml` is read when present. An explicit file that cannot be read is an error. |

Every key of the file — and its `CODEFANG_*` environment variable — sets
the **default** of one flag; the precedence is explicit flag > environment
> config file > compiled default. `--config /dev/null` runs with the
compiled defaults only. Keys nothing reads are ignored with one
`warning: ignoring unsupported config keys: …` line. See
[Configuration](configuration.md) for the key → flag table.

```bash
codefang run -a history/anomaly --config ./ci.codefang.yaml .
```

No checkpoint store, incremental cache or trace exporter is linked into the
binary, so the Go-era `--checkpoint`, `--checkpoint-dir`, `--resume`,
`--clear-checkpoint`, `--cache-dir`, `--no-cache` and `--debug-trace` flags
are removed; passing one fails as an unknown argument. A run always analyzes
the whole requested window — bound it with `--limit` / `--since`.

#### Errors

Every user error prints `Error: <message>` to stderr, leaves stdout empty and
exits 1:

| Situation | Message |
|-----------|---------|
| the path does not exist | `path not found: <path>` |
| a history analyzer on a directory that is not a git repository | `cannot open repository: <path>` |
| an unknown `--format` | `unsupported format: <value>` |
| a known format the selection cannot render (e.g. static-only `ndjson`, mixed `compact`) | `format <value> is not supported for <analyzer>` |
| an unknown analyzer id | `unknown analyzer id: <id>` |
| `--limit`, `--tick-size`, `--max-changes-per-commit`, `--granularity`, `--sampling`, `--typos-max-distance`, `--anomaly-window`, `--anomaly-threshold`, `--min-comment-len` out of range | `invalid --<flag>: must be … , got <value>` |
| `--ndjson` without `--format timeseries` | `invalid --ndjson: requires --format timeseries, got --format <f>` |
| `--verbose` with `--quiet` | `--verbose and --quiet cannot be used together` |
| an unreadable `--config` file | `cannot read --config <path>: …` |
| a malformed config file or an out-of-range key | `invalid config <path>: <key> must be …, got <value>` (or the parser's message naming the key and line) |
| a malformed `CODEFANG_*` variable | `invalid environment variable <NAME>: …` |
| `-o` cannot be created | `cannot write --output <path>: …` |
| an unresolvable `--since` | `cannot resolve --since "<value>": …` |
| an unknown `--languages` token | `static --languages: unknown language: "<token>"` / `history --languages: …` |
| an unreadable `--people-dict` | `cannot read --people-dict <path>: …` |
| an analyzer produced nothing for an otherwise valid run | `no report produced for <analyzer> --format <format>` |

A history `--format text` selection that includes an analyzer without a text
renderer writes the header and the section name first, then fails with
`serialization error for <Name>: unsupported format: text`.

### `codefang version`

Prints `codefang <version> (commit: <hash>, built: <date>)`:

- `<version>` — the crate version (or `CF_VERSION` / `GIT_VERSION` set at
  build time);
- `<hash>` — the commit the binary was built from: `CF_COMMIT` /
  `GIT_COMMIT` / `GIT_HASH` set at build time, else the `HEAD` of the
  checkout it was built in, else `unknown`;
- `<date>` — `CF_DATE` / `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` set at build time, else
  `unknown` (the build never reads the wall clock).

```bash
codefang version
```

The former `codefang render <store-dir>` subcommand only ever printed
"not available" — there is no stored-report format to render from — and is
removed; `codefang run --format plot -o <dir>` writes the HTML pages
directly.

### `codefang completion <shell>`

Generates the shell-completion script for `bash`, `fish`, `powershell` or
`zsh` on stdout, from the live command tree (every flag on this page).
`--no-descriptions` leaves the help texts out of the script.

```bash
codefang completion bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/codefang
```

---

### MCP server

The Model Context Protocol server lives in the `cf-mcp` crate. It exposes
Codefang analysis capabilities as tools that AI agents can discover and invoke
over stdio:

| Tool | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `codefang_analyze` | Static code analysis (complexity, cohesion, halstead, comments, imports) |
| `codefang_history` | Git history analysis (burndown, couples, devs, sentiment, etc.) |
| `uast_parse` | Parse source code into Universal AST |

The crate is a library: the `codefang` binary has no `mcp` subcommand in
this release. See the [MCP Integration](../integrations/mcp.md) guide for the
tool reference.

---

## `uast`

The UAST binary parses source files into a Universal Abstract Syntax Tree and
provides querying, diffing, and exploration utilities. The root command has
no flags of its own; every flag below belongs to its subcommand and is read by
it (`uast <command> --help` lists the same set).

### `uast parse`

Parse one or more source files into UAST format.

```bash
uast parse [files...] [flags]
```

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--language` | `-l` | `string` | `""` | Force language detection override |
| `--output` | `-o` | `string` | `""` | Output file (default: stdout) |
| `--format` | `-f` | `string` | `json` | Output format: `json` (pretty), `compact` (one line per input), `none` (parse only) |
| `--all` | | `bool` | `false` | Parse all source files in the codebase recursively |

With no files (and no `--all`), or for a `-` file argument, the source is read
from stdin and parsed as Go unless `-l` names the language. With `-o`, every
input's document is written to the one file, in input order.

```bash
# Parse a single file
uast parse main.go

# Parse all Go files, one compact document per line
uast parse -f compact *.go

# Force language detection
uast parse -l go main.c

# Read from stdin
cat main.go | uast parse -

# Save to file
uast parse -o output.json main.go

# Parse entire codebase
uast parse --all
```

---

### `uast query`

Query UAST nodes using the functional DSL.

```bash
uast query <expression> [files...] [flags]
```

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--input` | `-i` | `string` | `""` | Input file (UAST JSON or source code), queried before any positional files |
| `--output` | `-o` | `string` | `""` | Output file (default: stdout); every input's result is written to it, in input order |
| `--format` | `-f` | `string` | `json` | Output format: `json`, `compact`, `count` |
| `--interactive` | `-t` | `bool` | `false` | Interactive query mode over one file (`--input`, else the single positional file, else source read from stdin) |

With neither files nor `--input`, or for a `-` file argument, the query runs
over a UAST JSON tree read from stdin.

```bash
# Find the top-level functions (filter looks at the file's direct children)
uast query "filter(.type == 'Function')" main.go

# Find every function-role node anywhere in the tree, methods included
uast query 'rfilter(.roles has "Function")' main.go

# The name of every declaration in the tree
uast query "rmap(.props.name)" main.go

# Find exported items
uast query "filter(.roles has 'Exported')" *.go

# Count all nodes
uast query "reduce(count)" main.go

# Query from piped UAST JSON
uast parse main.go | uast query "filter(.type == 'Call')" -

# The same query over an --input file
uast query "filter(.type == 'Call')" -i main.go

# Count format
uast query -f count "filter(.type == 'Function')" main.go

# Interactive mode
uast query -t main.go
```

??? info "DSL Syntax Reference"

    A query is a pipeline of stages joined by `|`. `filter` and `map` look
    at their input set only — a `filter(...)` at the start of a query runs
    over the root's **direct children** — while `rfilter` and `rmap` apply
    the same predicate / expression to every node of each input's subtree in
    pre-order (the input itself first).

    | Expression | Description |
    |-----------|-------------|
    | `filter(.type == "Function")` | Direct children of the root whose type is `Function` |
    | `rfilter(.type == "Call")` | Every function call anywhere in the tree |
    | `rfilter(.type == "Identifier")` | Every identifier |
    | `rfilter(.roles has "Function")` | Every function-role node (functions and methods) |
    | `filter(.roles has "Exported")` | Direct children carrying a role |
    | `rfilter(.type == "Class") \| map(.props.name)` | The names of the classes |
    | `rmap(.props.name)` | The `name` property of every node that has one |
    | `map(.children)` | The children of each input node |
    | `reduce(count)` | Count the matching nodes |

    Field access resolves `children`, `token`, `id`, `roles`, `type`,
    `props`, `first`, `last`; any other name reads that property
    (`.props.name` ≡ `.name`). Comparisons: `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`,
    `>=`, `has` (membership in `roles`). Builtins: `contains`,
    `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `has`, `count`, `first`, `last`, `sort`.

---

### `uast diff`

Compare two files at the UAST structural level and report changes.

```bash
uast diff <file1> <file2> [flags]
```

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--output` | `-o` | `string` | `""` | Output file (default: stdout) |
| `--format` | `-f` | `string` | `unified` | Output format: `unified`, `summary`, `json` |

```bash
# Unified diff output (default)
uast diff old.go new.go

# Summary of change types
uast diff -f summary old.go new.go

# Machine-readable JSON
uast diff -f json old.go new.go

# Save to file
uast diff -o changes.json -f json old.go new.go
```

---

### `uast explore`

Start an interactive session for exploring the UAST structure of a file.

```bash
uast explore [file] [flags]
```

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--language` | `-l` | `string` | `""` | Force language detection override |

```bash
uast explore main.go
```

Available interactive commands:

| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `tree` | Show AST tree structure |
| `stats` | Show node type statistics |
| `find <type>` | Find nodes by type |
| `query <dsl>` | Execute a DSL query |
| `help` | Show available commands |
| `quit` | Exit exploration |

---

### `uast analyze`

Quick analysis shortcut that parses and analyzes source files in one step.

```bash
uast analyze [files...] [flags]
```

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--output` | `-o` | `string` | `""` | Output file (default: stdout) |
| `--format` | `-f` | `string` | `text` | Output format: `text`, `json`, `html` |

```bash
# Analyze a single file
uast analyze main.go

# Analyze all Go files as JSON
uast analyze -f json *.go

# Generate an HTML report
uast analyze -o report.html -f html *.go
```

---

### `uast validate`

Validate a UAST JSON document against the UAST JSON Schema. Exit codes: `0`
valid, `1` the document violates the schema, `2` an error (unreadable input,
malformed JSON, unreadable schema).

```bash
uast validate <file.json|-> [flags]
```

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--schema` | | `string` | `""` | Path to a UAST JSON schema; empty validates against the schema embedded in the binary |

```bash
# Validate a parsed tree against the embedded schema
uast parse -o tree.json main.go
uast validate tree.json
```

---

### `uast mapping`

Grammar helpers for UAST mapping authors: summarize and classify a
tree-sitter `node-types.json`, generate a `.uastmap` DSL skeleton from it, or
dump the raw tree-sitter tree of source files.

```bash
uast mapping [files...] [flags]
```

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Description |
|------|-------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--node-types` | | `string` | `""` | Path to `node-types.json` (required unless `--show-treesitter`) |
| `--format` | | `string` | `text` | Output format of the node-types summary: `text`, `json` |
| `--generate` | | `bool` | `false` | Print a `.uastmap` DSL skeleton generated from `node-types.json` |
| `--show-treesitter` | | `bool` | `false` | Print the raw tree-sitter tree (named nodes, positions, byte ranges, text) of each input file |
| `--language` | | `string` | `""` | Tree-sitter language name (e.g. `go`): required by `--show-treesitter`, written into the `--generate` header |
| `--extensions` | | `string` | `""` | Comma-separated file extensions written into the `--generate` header |

```bash
# Classify a grammar's node types
uast mapping --node-types node-types.json --format json

# Generate a mapping skeleton
uast mapping --node-types node-types.json --generate --language go --extensions .go

# Dump the tree-sitter tree of a file
uast mapping --show-treesitter --language go main.go
```

---

### `uast completion <shell>`

Generates the completion script for `bash`, `zsh`, `fish` or `powershell` on
stdout, covering every subcommand and flag listed on this page.

### `uast version`

Prints `uast <version> (commit: <hash>, built: <date>)`.

# File: site/explanation/complexity.md

# Understanding complexity metrics

This page explains the mental model behind the complexity analyzer: what
each metric means, the exact counting rules, how cyclomatic and cognitive
complexity differ, and how the rules are validated. For the output schema
and the thresholds, see the [Complexity reference](../analyzers/complexity.md).

---

## What it measures

The complexity analyzer measures three dimensions of code complexity from
source code: **cyclomatic complexity**, **cognitive complexity**, and
**nesting depth**, plus the **lines of code** of each function. It operates
on the UAST representation of your source files, with the file's source text
at hand so operators, identifiers and line counts can be recovered where a
language mapping does not carry them.

### Cyclomatic complexity (McCabe, 1976)

Counts the number of linearly independent paths through a function's
control-flow graph. The same rules apply to every language:

- Base score is `1`
- `+1` per `if`, `else if` / `elif`, and conditional (ternary) expression
- `+1` per loop (`for`, `while`, `do`, `loop`, `for … in`, `range`)
- `+1` per non-default `case` / match arm (`default`, `_`, `else` and
  Python's `case _:` add nothing)
- `+1` per `catch` / `except`
- `+1` per logical operator (`&&`, `||`, `and`, `or`)

!!! info "Interpretation"
    - **1-10**: Simple, low risk
    - **11-20**: Moderate complexity
    - **21-50**: High complexity, consider refactoring
    - **51+**: Very high risk, untestable

### Cognitive complexity (SonarSource, 2017)

Measures how difficult code is for a human to read and understand. Unlike
cyclomatic complexity, it penalizes nested structures more heavily and
rewards linear sequences of logic.

- **Structural increments**: `if`, conditional expressions,
  `switch`/`match`, loops and `catch` each add `1` **plus the current
  nesting level**, and raise the nesting level for what they contain.
- **Flat increments**: `else` and `else if` add `1` each and never a nesting
  penalty; an `else if` chain stays at the level of its first `if`.
- **Sequences of logical operators**: `+1` per run of like operators —
  `a && b && c` is one, `a && b || c` is two. A sequence is counted once
  wherever it appears (conditions, returns, assignments, call arguments).
- **Jumps to a label**: `break label`, `continue label` and `goto` add `1`;
  a plain `break`/`continue` adds nothing.
- **Direct recursion**: a call to the function itself adds `1`.
- **Nesting only**: lambdas and anonymous function literals (closures,
  callbacks) add nothing themselves but raise the nesting level for what
  they contain. `try` adds nothing; its `catch` is a structural increment.
- The function's own body is nesting level 0 — including an arrow or
  function-expression wrapper such as `const f = (x) => { … }`.
- A **named nested function** (Python `def` inside `def`, an inner `fn`,
  `const g = function () {}`) is its own unit: it is reported separately and
  excluded from the enclosing function's metrics.

### Nesting depth

The maximum depth of nested control-flow blocks within a function: each
`if`/`else` chain (one level for the whole chain), loop, `switch`/`match`
and `try`/`catch` statement (one level for the whole statement) opens a
level. Conditional expressions and lambdas are not blocks and do not count.
Deep nesting is a strong signal for refactoring.

### Lines of code and density

Lines of code are the non-blank lines of the function's span that carry
something other than comment text (comment-only lines and blank lines are
skipped; a trailing comment does not blank a code line). The lines of a
nested named function belong to that function. `complexity_density` is
cyclomatic complexity divided by lines of code.

---

## Counting rules

### What is a function

A `Function`/`Method` node with a body: a block, an expression body, or an
anonymous function/lambda it wraps (JS declarations). Declarations without a
body — C prototypes and declarators, Go function types and interface
methods, Rust trait signatures, Java abstract and interface methods — are
never reported. Anonymous function literals inside a function belong to
that function (they raise nesting); at the top level they are reported as
`anonymous` only when the mapping exposes them as functions.

Names come from the mapping's `name` property, else from the `Name`-role
identifier (through a C declarator), falling back to the identifier's source
text; a multi-line token is never a name.

### Worked example

```go
func decisions(a, b int, xs []int) int {
	r := 0
	if a > 0 && b > 0 {        // cyclomatic +1 (if) +1 (&&) | cognitive +1 (if) +1 (&& sequence)
		r++
	} else if a < 0 || b < 0 { // cyclomatic +1 (if) +1 (||) | cognitive +1 (else if) +1 (|| sequence)
		r--
	} else {                   //                           | cognitive +1 (else)
		r = 2
	}
	for _, x := range xs {     // cyclomatic +1              | cognitive +1
		r += x
	}
	switch r {                 //                           | cognitive +1
	case 1:                    // cyclomatic +1
		r = 10
	case 2:                    // cyclomatic +1
		r = 20
	default:                   // nothing
		r = 0
	}
	return r
}
```

Cyclomatic `1 + 7 = 8`, cognitive `7`, nesting depth `1` (nothing is nested
inside another block), lines of code `22`.

Nesting changes the cognitive score but not the cyclomatic one:

```go
func nested(a, b, c bool) int {
	if a {                 // cognitive +1 (nesting 0)
		if b {             // cognitive +2 (nesting 1)
			if c {         // cognitive +3 (nesting 2)
				return 1
			}
		}
	}
	return 0
}
```

Cyclomatic `4`, cognitive `6`, nesting depth `3`.

### Operator recovery

A binary operator is read from the node's `operator` property when the
language mapping provides one, else from the node's own token when that is
a bare operator symbol, else from the source text between the two operands.
Python's `and`/`or` are recognised through the same source-text rule even
where the mapping lowers them to a generic node.

---

## Validation

The counting rules are pinned by hand-computed fixtures, not by another
tool's output:

- `crates/cf-complexity/tests/fixtures/` holds Go, Python, JavaScript, Rust,
  Java and C sources (else-if chains, nested `else`, boolean sequences,
  `if` with an init statement, `try`/`catch`, lambdas and closures,
  `switch` with several cases, `default`/`_` arms, recursion, labelled
  jumps, nested functions, declarations without bodies, generics). Every
  function's cyclomatic, cognitive, nesting and line count is asserted
  from the parsed source (`crates/cf-complexity/tests/fixtures.rs`).
- `bins/codefang/tests/complexity_e2e.rs` drives the real binary over the
  same sources and asserts the exact numbers in `json`, `yaml`, `bin` and
  `text`, that `--per-file` entries sum to the aggregate, that every format
  survives 20 000 nesting levels, and that output is deterministic.
- Unit tests pin each rule on hand-built trees (`crates/cf-complexity/src`).

One expectation is recorded but not yet enforced: Java `switch` arms and
the Java ternary are lowered by the present mapping in a shape the analyzer
cannot count (`java_decisions_method` is `#[ignore]`d until the UAST mapping
contract lands); every other Java construct is covered.

---

## Use cases

- **Code review gates**: Reject pull requests where any function exceeds a cyclomatic complexity threshold.
- **Refactoring prioritization**: Sort functions by cognitive complexity to find the hardest-to-understand code.
- **Technical debt tracking**: Monitor complexity trends across releases.
- **Test planning**: Functions with high cyclomatic complexity need more test cases for full path coverage.

---

## Limitations

- **Language coverage**: Only languages supported by the UAST parser are analyzed. Unsupported files are silently skipped.
- **Mapping fidelity**: the analyzer counts what the language mapping exposes. Where a mapping lowers a construct to a generic node (with the present mapping: Java `switch` arms and the Java ternary), that construct is not counted until the mapping is fixed.
- **Generated code**: The analyzer does not distinguish hand-written code from generated code. Consider excluding generated directories (the default path policy already skips vendored and generated paths).
- **Macros and metaprogramming**: Complexity within macros or template metaprogramming may not be fully captured, since the UAST represents the source as written, not as expanded.
- **Cognitive complexity model**: The cognitive complexity scoring follows the SonarSource specification. Other tools may use slightly different weightings (for example, `gocognit` does not count `goto`).

---

## See also

- [Complexity reference](../analyzers/complexity.md) — output schema and thresholds.
- [Quick start](../getting-started/quickstart.md) — run your first analysis.


---

# File: site/explanation/cohesion.md

# Understanding cohesion metrics

This page explains the mental model behind the cohesion analyzer: what
counts as a variable, what LCOM-HS measures, how the variable-sharing ratio
captures communicational cohesion, how scores are combined across files, and
how to read them. For the output schema, see the
[Cohesion reference](../analyzers/cohesion.md).

---

## What it measures

The cohesion analyzer computes **LCOM-HS (Henderson-Sellers)** per file and a
**variable sharing ratio** per function to identify files whose functions are
poorly related to each other — a strong signal for refactoring.

Both metrics are built on one relation: *which function uses which
variable*. Everything below follows from how that relation is extracted.

### What counts as a variable

A function *uses* a variable when its body contains an identifier that reads
or writes it. The analyzer works lexically on the UAST — no symbol
resolution — with these rules:

| Counted | Not counted |
|---|---|
| Local variables (`x := 1`, `let m = …`, `const total = …`) — by the declared **name**, never the whole statement | Type names (`int`, `string`, `Config`, `i32`, `Self`, `number`) |
| Parameters (`cfg`, `items`, `n`) | The function's own name and its return-type annotation |
| Fields and attributes (`s.a` counts `a`; `self.x` counts `x`; `this.b` counts `b`) | Callees: `helper()`, `string(v)`, the `Println` in `fmt.Println(x)`, the `Validate` in `cfg.Validate()` |
| The object of a member access (`cfg` in `cfg.Name`, `fmt` in `fmt.Println`) | The receiver: `self`, `this`, and a Go receiver such as `s` in `func (s *S) M()` |
| Variables of a closure, attributed to the enclosing function | Literals (`1`, `"x"`, `nil`, `true`) |

Each function's variables form a **set**: using `x` three times is one use of
`x`.

!!! note "Lexical means lexical"
    `fmt` in `fmt.Println(x)` is indistinguishable from a variable without
    symbol resolution, so it counts. Two different variables that share a
    name across functions count as the same variable. Both are documented
    limitations, not bugs.

### LCOM-HS (lack of cohesion of methods — Henderson-Sellers)

LCOM-HS is the industry-standard cohesion metric used by NDepend, JArchitect,
and CppDepend.

**Formula (per file):**

```text
LCOM = 1 - sum(mA) / (m × a)
```

Where:

- `m` = number of functions in the file **that use at least one variable**
- `a` = number of distinct variables across those functions
- `mA` = for each variable, the number of functions that use it
- `sum(mA)` = the number of (function, variable) usage pairs

**Range:** 0.0 (perfect cohesion: every function uses every variable) to
1.0 (no cohesion: no two functions share a variable).

Functions that use no variables are not part of the usage matrix (there is
nothing they could share), so trivial helpers never penalize a file. When
fewer than two functions use a variable — a single-function file, or a file
of parameterless helpers — there is nothing to compare, and `LCOM = 0`.

**Worked example** — `f` uses `{x, y}`, `g` uses `{x}`:

```text
m = 2, a = 2 ({x, y}), sum(mA) = 2 (x) + 1 (y) = 3
LCOM = 1 - 3 / (2 × 2) = 0.25
```

### Cohesion score

A convenience inversion of LCOM-HS: `cohesion_score = 1.0 - LCOM`. Higher is
better. It drives the section score (`6/10` means `0.6`) and the summary
message:

| Cohesion score | Summary |
|---|---|
| ≥ 0.7 | Excellent overall cohesion across all analyzed code |
| ≥ 0.4 | Good overall cohesion with room for improvement |
| ≥ 0.3 | Fair overall cohesion - consider refactoring some functions |
| < 0.3 | Poor overall cohesion - significant refactoring recommended |

### Function-level cohesion (variable sharing ratio)

For each function, the analyzer computes what fraction of its variables is
shared with **at least one other function in the same file**. This measures
**communicational cohesion** (Yourdon-Constantine level 5).

**Formula:**

```text
function_cohesion = shared_vars / unique_vars
```

Where:

- `unique_vars` = the function's distinct variables
- `shared_vars` = those of them that at least one *other* function of the
  file also uses (a repeat inside the same function is not sharing)
- Functions with no variables score 1.0 (trivial, no penalty)
- Every function of a file with fewer than two variable-using functions
  scores 1.0 (nothing to compare against)

**Range:** 0.0 (completely isolated function) to 1.0 (all variables shared).

| Function cohesion | Assessment |
|---|---|
| ≥ 0.6 | Excellent — function shares most variables with the module |
| ≥ 0.4 | Good — reasonable sharing with room for improvement |
| ≥ 0.3 | Fair — consider refactoring |
| < 0.3 | Poor — function is isolated from the module |

Functions below **Excellent** are listed as issues, worst first. The
distribution counts every function in exactly one of the four buckets, so it
always sums to **Total Functions**.

In the worked example above, `f` shares `x` but not `y` (`0.5`, Good) and `g`
shares its only variable (`1.0`, Excellent).

### Across files

A variable is a per-file notion, so LCOM is never recomputed over a whole
tree. Instead:

- **LCOM Score** = the function-weighted mean of the per-file LCOM values (a
  file with five functions weighs five times a file with one);
- **Cohesion Score** = `1 - LCOM Score`;
- **Avg Cohesion** = the mean per-function cohesion over every function;
- **Total Functions** = every function found. Same-named functions are kept
  (methods are reported as `Type.name`, e.g. `A.String` and `B.String`).

Files without functions — struct-only files, empty files, Markdown — carry
**no cohesion data**: they are excluded from every denominator. A tree in
which no file has a function reports `No cohesion data available` with score
`0/10` (and exit code 0). Use `--per-file` to see each file's own LCOM.

---

## Per-language notes

- **Go** — `type_identifier` nodes (`int`, `Config`) are typed and excluded;
  receivers are excluded and name the method (`S.M1`); closures (`func()
  {…}` literals) belong to the enclosing function.
- **Python** — `self` is excluded; methods are qualified by their class
  (`C.m1`); decorators are outside the function. Type annotations are plain
  identifiers in Python's UAST and therefore count.
- **JavaScript / TypeScript** — `this` is excluded; class methods are
  qualified (`A.m1`); TypeScript type annotations are excluded.
- **Java** — `this` is excluded; methods, including constructors, are
  qualified by their class (`A.m1`, `A.A`); primitive types are excluded.
- **Rust** — `self` is excluded; `impl` blocks do not qualify method names
  (`m1`, not `S.m1`). Identifier nodes in the Rust mapping carry no token;
  their names are recovered from the enclosing function's source span.
- Any language supported by the UAST works; results are best where variable
  declarations and function definitions are explicit.

---

## Use cases

- **Refactoring targets**: Find functions with low sharing ratio that do unrelated work and should be split.
- **Architecture reviews**: Validate that files follow the Single Responsibility Principle by checking LCOM-HS scores.
- **Code quality tracking**: Monitor cohesion trends over time to catch degradation.
- **Code review**: Use per-function cohesion scores to identify newly added functions that lack cohesion with existing code.

---

## Methodology references

- **LCOM-HS**: Henderson-Sellers, B. (1996). *Object-Oriented Metrics: Measures of Complexity*. Prentice Hall. The Henderson-Sellers variant normalizes LCOM to [0, 1] and is the variant used by NDepend, JArchitect, and CppDepend.
- **Variable Sharing Ratio**: Measures communicational cohesion per the Yourdon-Constantine classification. A function that shares all its variables with other functions in the module exhibits high communicational cohesion.

---

## Limitations

- **Lexical names**: The analyzer uses identifier spellings. Different variables with the same name across functions count as shared; package qualifiers (`fmt`) count as variables.
- **Constructors and initializers**: A constructor that initializes every field (`S { a: 1, b: 2 }`, `this.a = …`) uses every field and ties the other methods together, raising the file's cohesion.
- **Accessor methods**: Simple getters/setters may inflate cohesion since each touches only one shared field.
- **Single-function files**: Files with only one function always receive perfect cohesion (LCOM = 0.0, cohesion = 1.0) since there are no other functions to compare against.
- **Trivial functions**: Functions with no variables receive a cohesion score of 1.0 to avoid penalizing simple utility functions.

---

## See also

- [Cohesion reference](../analyzers/cohesion.md) — output schema and thresholds.
- [Quick start](../getting-started/quickstart.md) — run your first analysis.


---

# File: site/explanation/halstead.md
